craft_claim: Deadpan works by withholding the play signal: the writer never announces the joke, so the reader must infer that a play frame is active. The inference is the mechanism; removing it converts comedy into literal statement.

supporting_evidence.location: in Bateson (ed.), *A Theory of Play and Fantasy*, pp. 31–56
supporting_evidence.note: Bateson's play signal marks 'these are not the signals that they would be' — deadpan is defined by the removal of exactly this marker, requiring the participant to reframe unprompted. Tier 2, foundational theoretical paper.
Frame analysis explains the reader's re-framing work: a neutral surface must be reclassified as 'this is play/satire' using keys supplied elsewhere in the text. Tier 2 scholarly book.

Winner documents that detecting nonliteral, teasing, or ironic intent is a learned competence — readers who lack the competence never enter the play frame. Tier 2 scholarly book; supports both the mechanism and failure mode (claim 5).

counterevidence.note: Clark and Gerrig treat obviousness as a spectrum: pretense can be partially transparent, and audiences may knowingly go along with an obvious pretense. Bounds the claim: deadpan occupies the *least obvious* end but the frame need not be fully hidden for irony to work.

scope: Written contexts where no performer is present to signal with face or timing. Holds for narration, essay, and dialogue; in stage/film media some signals (Keaton's face) are present but still minimal.
exceptions: When the text supplies an early unmistakable 'tell' (an incongruity that cannot be sincere), the frame is inferred quickly and reliably; when no key exists at all, the reader stays literal (claims 5 and 9).
